Empirical Research Plan – Taxable-Income Elasticity in the 1980s U.S. Tax Reforms  

==============================================================

1. Identification Strategy  
--------------------------------  
Preferred approach: Two‐way-fixed-effects (TWFE) panel regression of (log) taxable income on the net-of-tax rate (= 1 – MTR), estimated by two‐stage least squares (2SLS).  
• Stage 1: Instrument the actual marginal tax rate (MTR_it) with a “simulated” marginal tax rate (SMTR_it) that depends only on tax-law changes, not on contemporaneous income.  
• Stage 2: Use the predicted MTR to recover the elasticity of taxable income (ETI).  
Rationale  
a. Reforms generate large, discontinuous changes in statutory rates that differ by year and income bracket ⇒ strong relevance.  
b. Because SMTR_it is constructed from last year’s real income run through the new schedule, it is orthogonal to current-year income shocks ⇒ plausibly exogenous.  
c. The 1979–1990 individual panel allows taxpayer and year fixed effects, mitigating time-invariant heterogeneity and aggregate shocks.  
The 2SLS panel with FE combines the strengths of Difference-in-Differences (time variation) and IV (addressing mechanical endogeneity of the statutory schedule).

2. Treatment and Control Definition  
-------------------------------------------  
Treatment Variable  
• Continuous: Δ ln(1 – MTR_it) (or its level); policy interest is β = elasticity of taxable income.  
Instrument  
• SMTR_it = statutory marginal rate taxpayer i would face in year t if her real taxable income stayed at its t–1 level.  
Control / Counterfactual  
• Taxpayers whose SMTR changes little (or in the opposite direction) serve as contemporaneous controls. Within-year identification comes from cross-sectional variation; across-year identification comes from reform dates.  
Treatment Timing  
• Main events: ERTA 1981 (takes effect 1982–84) and TRA 1986 (big change effective 1987–88). We keep the full 1979–1990 panel and absorb each year’s aggregate shock with year FE.  
(If one prefers a cleaner DID/event-study complement, define “treated” = top-bracket filers whose statutory MTR fell ≥ 10 pp in 1987; controls = middle-bracket filers whose rates changed ≤ 2 pp.)

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
-------------------------------------  
A1 (Instrument relevance): Reforms induce substantial cross-taxpayer variation in SMTR_it. Plausible and testable (first-stage F ≫ 10 expected).  
A2 (Instrument exogeneity): Conditional on taxpayer FE, year FE, and macro controls, SMTR_it is uncorrelated with contemporaneous income shocks. Reasonable because it uses lagged income and statutory schedule only.  
A3 (Stable unit treatment): One taxpayer’s tax rate does not affect another’s taxable income (no externalities at this horizon). Plausible.  
A4 (No differential trends within income groups): For the DID/event-study interpretation, absent the reform, income growth of high- versus low-change groups would have been parallel. Plausible given short windows; can be probed with pre-trend tests.  
A5 (Reporting vs. real income): We implicitly treat reported income as choice variable responsive to MTR. If evasion/avoidance behavior differs systematically across groups outside the reform, estimates could capture compliance as well as real labor supply. Need interpretation caution.

4. Main Threats & Remedies  
--------------------------------  
T1 Mean reversion / income dynamics. High-income taxpayers may experience natural declines, creating spurious negative relation to MTR cuts.  
➔ Include taxpayer FE and control for lagged income growth; run specification in first differences; exclude extreme transitory income spikes.  
  
T2 Concurrent base-broadening provisions (especially TRA 86) change deductions/credits, affecting taxable income independent of MTR.  
➔ Control flexibly for itemized-deduction eligibility, filing status, and use alternative dependent variable (AGI); run robustness dropping years 1987–88 or focusing on ERTA episode.  
  
T3 Inter-temporal income shifting (timing avoidance) around reform years, biasing short-run estimates.  
➔ Estimate both short-run (t, t+1) and medium-run (t+2, t+3) elasticities; include event-time dummies to visualize transitory spikes; smooth income with 3-year moving average in robustness.

5. R Code Outline  
-----------------------  
```r
# Packages
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)   # fast FE + IV
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

# 1. Load data ----------------------------------------------------------
tax <- read_csv("irs_1979_1990.csv")   # assume wide panel

# 2. Basic variable construction ---------------------------------------
tax <- tax %>% 
  arrange(taxpayer_id, year) %>%
  group_by(taxpayer_id) %>%
  mutate(
    # Net-of-tax rate
    netoftax = 1 - mtr,                       # actual marginal tax rate
    lnit     = log(taxable_income),
    # Simulated marginal tax rate (instrument)
    smtr     = lead(mtr_static, default = NA) # placeholder; normally:
    # smtr_t = statutory MTR in year t applied to real (CPI-adjusted) income from year t-1
  ) %>% 
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(ln_netoftax = log(netoftax),
         ln_smtr     = log(1 - smtr))

# 3. Estimation sample --------------------------------------------------
sample <- tax %>% 
  filter(!is.na(smtr), taxable_income > 0)

# 4. Main 2SLS FE specification ----------------------------------------
#   ln(Y_it) = α_i + δ_t + β * ln(1 - MTR_it) + ε_it
est_main <- feols(lnit ~ 1 | taxpayer_id + year | 
                    ln_netoftax ~ ln_smtr, 
                  data = sample, cluster = ~taxpayer_id)

summary(est_main)

# 5. Robustness: (i) exclude 1986–88 transition years -------------------
rob1 <- sample %>% filter(!year %in% 1986:1988)
est_rob1 <- feols(lnit ~ 1 | taxpayer_id + year | 
                    ln_netoftax ~ ln_smtr, 
                  data = rob1, cluster = ~taxpayer_id)
summary(est_rob1)

# 6. Robustness: event-study pre-trends around TRA 86 -------------------
#  Create relative‐year indicators
event <- tax %>% 
  mutate(rel_year = year - 1987) %>%
  filter(rel_year >= -5 & rel_year <= 5) %>%
  mutate(rel_year_fct = factor(rel_year))

est_event <- feols(lnit ~ i(rel_year_fct, ref = "-1") | taxpayer_id, 
                   data = event, cluster = ~taxpayer_id)
iplot(est_event)
```

6. Expected Results  
-------------------------  
Theory (labor supply + avoidance) predicts taxable income rises when marginal tax rates fall ⇒ positive elasticity with respect to net-of-tax rate.  
Existing estimates for the 1980s place ETI in the 0.2–0.4 range for high-income filers; middle-income elasticities are lower (≈ 0.1). I therefore expect:  
β ≈ 0.25 overall, ≈ 0.35 for the top decile.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Instrumental-Variables Panel)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------------  
C1 Strong first-stage (F > 10) ……… 1  
C2 Exogeneity of instrument ………… 0.8 (some concern about income anticipation)  
C3 No simultaneous policy shocks ….. 0.7 (base broadening partially addressed)  
C4 No differential pre-trends ……….. 0.9 (to be tested via event-study)  
C5 Stable unit treatment ………………. 1  

Average score ≈ 0.88 – credible but requires robustness exercises outlined above.
